utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President; good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefan Bourgon, co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet every one present, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else either in or around the courtroom. We have a witness scheduled for today, but before we call the witness into the courtroom, could the Defence counsel tell me whether I've understood you correctly. The witness scheduled for tomorrow was not initially included in the official list, as you know, for witnesses, and on official list, as a rule it's necessary to ask for leave to amend the list in order to introduce a new witness. So could you clarify this subject, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do apologise. We made an error when we told you that the witness wasn't on the list on Friday. He was on the list, but we hadn't obtained confirmation from him that he would be appearing, that is to say that he would be testifying. He confirmed he would be testifying on Saturday. We the informed Prosecution of this. We informed them that the witness would be appearing before the Trial Chamber tomorrow. He comes from a European country, one of the European countries, and since he has requested certain protective measures, we'll inform the Trial Chamber of the measures requested tomorrow. But for the moment, I wouldn't like to mention his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. As far as the witness who will be testifying is concerned, how much time do you think you will need to examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our examination should take an hour and a half, but I think the examination-in-chief will last between an hour and an hour and a half, no longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. Let's go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we are back in open session, let's call the witness into the courtroom. Could the usher bring the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure you're receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. So please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date of birth and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Redzib Begic. I was born on the 23rd of February, 1956, in Zenica, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently employed, and if so, what is your profession? What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a lawyer, and I work in a company at the moment, a trade company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind, and if so, what position did you hold and where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was the chief of the security services centre in Zenica as part of the Ministry of the Interior in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of 1993, up until February, I held that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was appointed as a Judge of the high court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were a Judge until when exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until January of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] January 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to the events that occurred in your country between 1992 and 1993 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we'll be following here. As you were a Judge for over ten years, you will not be surprised by what I tell you. According to the procedure we follow here, you will first have to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel. You must have met them this weekend. You must have seen them this weekend. They're to your left. Their examination should take between an hour and an hour and a half. They will be conducting what we call their examination-in-chief. After they have concluded their examination-in-chief, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will conduct their cross-examination. This is a very common law procedure. You will soon notice that the questions put to you by Defence Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond counsel and the questions put to you by the Prosecution are not quite the same. After this stage has been completed, Defence counsel may re-examine you. Then the three Judges who are sitting before you may also ask you questions. The Rules allow the Judges to ask witnesses questions at any point in time, but we prefer to ask witnesses questions after both parties have finished asking witnesses their questions. You will see that our questions will be somewhat different than the questions put to you by the parties. As a rule, we ask witnesses questions to obtain certain clarifications and to fill in any gaps in your testimony. We will also have two breaks that will last between 25 and 30 minutes. We have these breaks for technical reasons and allow the witnesses to have a rest. As a Judge, you're aware of the fact that it is tiring for witnesses to answer questions, and this is why it is necessary for the witnesses to have a rest. As the procedure followed here is almost entirely oral, the witness's answers are very important, because your answers will be transcribed, and the transcription of your answers will be our evidence. We don't have any documents, any written documents. When a question is put to you, you may be shown a document and you may be asked to comment on the document. The Judges might also show you the documents that they have, since it these documents have already been admitted into evidence. I would also like to draw your attention to other important points. This won't surprise you, as you have taken the solemn declaration, this means you should not give false testimony. False testimony is an offence, and it is punishable. You could be given a fine or a sentence of up to five -- seven years in prison. Secondly, and this is characteristic of the common law system, when a witness is answering a question, if the witness believes that the information he provides might subsequently be used against him, the witness can refuse to answer the question. These are rules that exist in certain countries that follow the continental system. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber may obliged a witness to answer such a question, but the witness is granted a form of immunity. In common law countries, it's the Prosecution that grants this form of immunity. In this Tribunal, it's the Chamber that grants this form of immunity. If you fail to understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Sometimes the questions are complicated, and if that's the case, you should ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. I'll now give the floor to the Defence, who will provide you with additional information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Begic. As the Presiding Judge has already said, I would like to ask you to try and pause before you answer the questions I put to you, as we speak the same language. It is important for my questions and your answers to be interpreted so that everyone in the courtroom can follow our exchange. So please pause after I have put a question to you so my question can be interpreted, and then answer the question. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, can you tell me where you live now?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I live in Zenica in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Chamber, you said that you were a lawyer by profession. Could you tell me a little about your professional background?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: After I completed secondary school, I studied at the school of law in Sarajevo, at the department in Zenica. I graduated in 1979. I then took the bar examine. That was in 1982. I took the exam in Sarajevo, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said what position you held in 1992 and afterwards. Could you please tell me what you did before the war.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Before the war, as soon as I graduated, I was a trainee in the district court in Zenica, and I was preparing to take the bar exam. In 1982, I was elected as a Judge of what was then called the basic court in Zenica, and I was there until 1989. I was then appointed as a Judge at the high court in Zenica, and I worked as a Judge until July 1991, when I was appointed as the chief of the security services centre in Zenica. As I have already said, I held that position until the end of February 1993, and then I returned to the court. I was appointed as a Judge of the high court in Zenica again. And at the same time, I was a Judge at the Supreme Court in Sarajevo. I was replacing someone, and that was within the framework of the high court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, before the war did you serve in an army, and if so, which army and when?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served in the former JNA. That was in 1981, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you served in the army, did you obtain a rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When telling us about the duties you performed, you said that in April 1992, when the JNA and Serbian forces attacked the -- Bosnia-Herzegovina, you said you were in the Zenica Security Services Centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of the duties that you had, were you also a member of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The law on the armed forces or, rather, the decree law that regulated those matters, well, as a member of the Ministry of the Interior, I was considered a member of the armed forces as well, but this was only at a time of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, since the army was also -- also represented the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you tell me: What is the joint command for the security services centre and the army?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who was your superior organ, and who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior in Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, the Minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As head of the security services centre, tell me, what area did this centre cover?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: It covered the Zenica region, as it was known then. That is the region to the north, is a Vidovici, Zepca, Zenica, Kakanj, Vitez, Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Donji and Gornji Vakuf, and Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which organisational unit of the Ministry of the Interior insisted -- existed in those municipalities, and who were you superior to?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: In each of these municipalities, there were public security stations, and I was superior to the heads of those police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be able to follow your answers as we go along, could you tell us, as head of the security services centre, which aspect of security was your centre responsible for?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The competencies of the Ministry of the Interior were regulated by law on the organisation of the republican administration, and more specifically, by the Law on Internal Affairs. This law stipulated that the competencies of the Ministry of the Interior were primarily to protect public law and order, personal and property safety of citizens, and also, very importantly, to detect the perpetrators of crimes and submit criminal reports. This administrative/legal competence also included question of citizenship, issuance of travel documents, keeping records and controlling the movement of aliens, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, within the framework of the security services centre in Zenica, were there separate security sectors or departments which specialised in a particular aspect of security?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of the Ministry of Interior, there was the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond administration for state security, and similarly within the centre for security services there was a sector for state security which was directly subordinated to the under-secretary for state security or the deputy minister of internal affairs. So in addition to that sector, there was a public security sector which covered the areas that I listed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answering my previous question, you said that organs of the Ministry of the Interior or the civilian police, to put it briefly, and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a joint superior command which was, in fact, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were head of the security services centre, and later on when you worked as a Judge in a higher court of Zenica, was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the 3rd Corps superior to the security services centre?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, Mr. Begic, whether in addition to the regular police force that you had in peacetime, during the war were additional forces organised and, if so, tell us which and how.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Even before the war, a unit or units of the reserve police force were mobilised. This was not just during the war, but even before the war these units had been mobilised, which means before April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, you said that the centre of the security services was never subordinated or resubordinated to the 3rd Corps Bosnia-Herzegovina or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole. Tell me, did the law envisage the possibility for certain parts of the security centre to be placed under the command of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, if so, will you please explain?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: This referred to reserve units of the police who, by decision of the Minister of the Interior, could be resubordinated to the army command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was this on a permanent basis, a temporary basis, or some other basis that these forces were resubordinated? And when the requirement ceased what happened to those reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: These were occasionally resubordinated. And as soon as the need for them ceased, they would go back to their regular duties within the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about some duties within the terms of reference of the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, the security services centre, you said that some of its competencies were linked to the detection of criminal offences and their perpetrators. Tell me: In addition to the law you referred to a moment ago regulating the competence of bodies of the Ministry of Interior, were there any other laws regulating the conduct of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the law on criminal proceedings which specified more clearly the position and the role of the Ministry of the Interior in discovering perpetrators, in investigating and collecting information upon the request of the court or, rather, the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that one of the competencies of the Ministry of the Interior bodies had to do with the movement of aliens and registration of aliens. Tell me, was there an organisational unit within the security services centre in Zenica specially dealing with these issues?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the so-called department for foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any legal provision or practice on the basis of which some other state or military bodies might take over this responsibility from the organs of internal affairs or, rather, are you aware that that competence was ever taken away from bodies of internal affairs before or during or after the war?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that never occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you held an important position, that is head of the security services centre at the beginning of the war, tell me, did you encounter any problems when it -- when we're talking about relations with foreigners, and of what kind?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems, and it was very difficult for the department or foreigners to fulfil its role in that area. This was primarily due to the fact that at the very outset of the war, the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not be controlled by legal bodies so that when foreigners entered, and that is the most important moment when you want to monitor their movement, we didn't have information that a foreigner had entered Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you, who controlled the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The borders were controlled by bodies within Republika Srpska or bodies of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did any entry into Bosnia-Herzegovina or frontier crossing -- was any frontier crossing controlled by the legal MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina at any point along the border?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you. You said that there were many problems, the first being the inability to control the entry and registration of foreigners coming into the country. Could you mention the others? I think you said there were several.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the duty of all entities, both legal and physical entities, to report the arrival and sojourn of foreigners. Such reports never reached us. Now, whether this was due to the fact that those foreigners were not staying in hotels and information was most frequently passed on from hotels, now, whether it was due to that or to some other reason, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, in 1992, when Bosnia and Herzegovina was confronted with the war and the horrific consequences of that war, did foreigners come, and who were those foreigners?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: As a citizen, I am aware that there were foreigners. Later on, it emerged that some of those foreigners were registered by humanitarian organisations such as the association of citizens, Al Husamen [phoen] or others. According to the law on the association of citizens, the registration of associations was within the competence of courts. After registration, within the framework of those associations, those foreigners were free to act, too, quite legally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, did foreign journalists come to the area controlled by the security centre -- security services centre? Were they registered with you?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to tell you that no one registered with us, so none the foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, could one notice foreigners coming on an individual basis, or was this a period when large numbers of foreigners arrived of various origins?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: In that period was a period of major fluctuation of people, including people in uniform. In 1992, there would be times when hundreds of people would come to Zenica. Among them were those in uniform who were deserting their lines, fleeing from the war operations, and accompanying their families. To what extent foreigners were present is something I'm unable to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some humanitarian organisations. Could you tell us approximately how many various international or national humanitarian organisations were registered in Zenica at that year?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I'm really unable to tell you that, because I never had any such information or data. There are data about that in the registers of courts, but I know as a citizen that they were quite numerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the competencies of the security services centres, you said that one of your competencies was linked to the identification, personal documents, and the rest of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell me, in 1992 and 1993, did the composition of the population change, and did people come to Zenica from various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Certainly. One might say that it became the rule to move around without any ID papers. There were so many persons who may not even have had any such ID documents that we simply stopped checking people in that Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the problems you have referred to that you had to deal with, tell me: Did the security services centre at some point in time have to deal with the collapse of a part of the system or, rather, tell me, were you able to control the whole territory that you described for us a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Very soon after the beginning of the war, with the formation of the Croatian Defence council, public security stations that were located in areas where Croats had -- were in power even before the war, they in a sense eschewed control of the security centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown a set of documents so that I can move on to my next question linked to one of those documents. We have a sufficient number of copies for Their Honours, the Prosecution, and our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, could you please have a look at document number one. The Defence number which you can see at the top of the document is 0449. The date of the document is the 24th of August, 1992. Mr. Begic, I assume that you haven't seen this document before, but please tell me: Does this document show that areas under HVO control prevented the civilian police of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from carrying out their work, and they started doing this very early? Is this something that you are familiar with? Was this the case in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I've seen this order, but I knew that members of the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, I knew that men who were under me were not able to go to these areas, to areas under HVO control, because very soon the legal authorities in the public security stations soon merged with the HVO organisation. I could provide you with an example, Busovaca. I could mention Vitez as well. And the building of the public security station there was taken over by members either of the HVO or of the HOS. And then the same occurred in Zepca. Members of the MUP could not go to those areas without taking risks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As of that time, Mr. Begic, did your inspectors and policemen -- were your inspectors and policemen able to perform their duties in those areas? Could they carry out controls, conduct investigations, interview individuals, and carry out other police work?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No. No, they doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, in other municipalities such as Travnik and Bugojno, which were within the framework of your security services centre, were parallel organs, parallel police organs established, and did this make it difficult for the civilian police to perform all their duties?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, there was such a problem in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, could you now tell me whether you know that at some point in time in the territory where your civilian police operated the 3rd Corps was formed and BH army units?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, the 3rd Corps was formed towards the end of 1992. It included units -- it was composed of units that already existed at the time. In other words, it linked up units of BH army -- from the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the 3rd Corps was founded and developed, do you know whether certain police organs were formed within the corps?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as the 3rd Corps was formed, as far as I can remember, a military police battalion was formed too. It was part of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, could you tell me what sort of staff your security services centre had before the war and at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I can claim with full responsibility that we had staff who were capable of performing the duties they were supposed to perform in the Zenica security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the centre have the technical equipment they needed in order to carry out their work?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the department for crime technology, and they had the staff, and they had the equipment. They had sufficient equipment at the beginning of war to carry out investigations that had to be done in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, although a lot of this equipment was damaged in the wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that after the formation of the 3rd Corps, a military police battalion was formed within the 3rd Corps. Tell me, do you know what sort of equipment and men the military police battalion had at the time?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The military police battalion wasn't adequately equipped, and it didn't have an adequate staff to carry out its duties, and that's why cooperation was established between the Ministry of the Interior and the security -- or, rather, the security services centre in Zenica and the 3rd Corps. And quite frequently, in addition to the training that our members provided to members of the military police, our members would also become directly engaged and perform tasks for military security. Investigating judges from the district military court often requested assistance or, rather, from the district military prosecutor's office. So what the military police couldn't do would be done by members of our centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, can you remember whether at any point in time, at the beginning of 1993, a request was made by the 3rd Corps and by an investigating judge for your organs to carry out some of the investigations that concerned bringing in people who had been killed in the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that was in January 1993 at the request of the investigating judge from the district military court. We carried out certain investigations that involved examining corpses and performing a paraffin test on the bodies that were brought to the Zenica morgue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, to the best of your recollection was the military police battalion in a position to carry out those tasks since you said at that time they lacked the necessary equipment and they didn't have adequate staff?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, since the investigating judge from the military court requested that we carry out these activities, you can see that the members of the military police weren't in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at documents five, six, and seven now, and document number eight. Let's have a look at document number five first. The document is P332, document number P332. And could you first tell me whether this is a document from the security services centre of which you were the chief.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I signed as the chief of the security services centre. And certain notes were attached to this document, and certain findings. The findings from the paraffin test was attached to the document, and a photo record was attached, a photo record of unidentified bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number six now, document P333.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is this a document from your security services centre, and do you know who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an official note. It's a document from the Zenica security services centre and it was drafted by an employee of the crime technology department. His name is Redzo Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number seven. The number of the document is P334. Tell me, is this a document from the security services centre, and do you know the person who compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This document also comes from the security services centre, and the note was compiled by Enes Saric, who also worked in the department for crime technology.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document eight, document number P341, and tell me whether this is a document compiled by the security services centre, and do you know who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the Zenica Security Services Centre. It is the paraffin test expert analysis. It was signed by Hadzic Redzo, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond an employee in the department for crime technology, and I also signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, could you tell me who actually carried out these investigations in the security services centre? The men who carried these investigations out, were they professionals? Were they ordinary policemen? Could you tell us who carried out the investigations, and could you tell us what sort of equipment was used to carry out such an analysis?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that the people who did this were competent, and they had the adequate professional level and experience to carry out such work. And in particular, as far as the paraffin test is concerned, this test was done by someone who was a biologist by profession, and he had done such work for a long time before making this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, in the document which you have examined, document number P33 [as interpreted], it's document number six among the document that you have before you. In this document it says that Turkic Faruk, a pathologist, the Judges and the prosecutor of the Zenica military court and the Zenica CSB forensic officer were members of the identification team. Before I put my following question to you, could you tell me the following: On the basis your answer -- well, you said that you worked as a judge for most of your professional life. Which fields were you involved in as a judge? What sort of cases did you work on as a judge? What sort of cases did you try?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, these cases were criminal cases, and for the best part of my career as a Judge, I was involved in criminal cases. Only for a short period of time was I involved in other kinds of cases. That was while I was a Judge in the low court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. On page 21, line 17, the Prosecution number hasn't been correctly recorded. The number is 333 and not 33. I'll now go back to this document. Given your experience as a judge in criminal cases, could you tell me, when a judge is involved in an investigation who is in charge of the investigation? Who issues orders to carry out certain investigative actions? Who is, in fact, in charge of the entire situation?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the exclusive responsibility of the investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the judge takes over that work, so to speak, either in a pre-trial stage or either in an investigative stage, as the civilian police and as the military police, were you able to establish certain conditions? Were you able to conduct the investigation as you saw fit, apart from the way in which the court said the investigations should be conducted?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, after you -- after security services centre provided all the documents on the investigations carried out, the investigations that you were ordered to carry out by the court, and these were cases which involved the pre-trial phase, what was the investigative judge supposed to do with all the documents that were gathered at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, all -- all the documents, all the evidence had to be provided by the judge to the Prosecutor. It was necessary to assess whether it was a crime. It was necessary to decide whose responsibility the crime was. And then the results should be provided to the prosecutor. Generally speaking, the investigative judge from the district military court forwarded all the results of investigations to the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this note signed by your employee Redzo Hadzic, the number of which is P333, you can see that in addition to the judge, the prosecutor of the district military court in Zenica was also present. On the basis of your experience as a -- as a judge, could you tell us to whom this document was provided by the judge who was involved in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: He would with only provide this to the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, once the prosecutor's office receives all the documents established by the investigating judge, either by procuring them himself or from the police and other bodies, who is then in charge of the pre-trial and trial stages?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Once the preliminary results of the investigations are passed on to the prosecutor, he is the only one who will decide whether he will file a request for an investigation or whether he might request the necessary information to be collected by the police, or if he finds that there's no reasonable grounds to suspect a crime having been committed, then the case will be filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Begic, if the police, be it the military or the civilian police, if in addition to the documents they were to file a criminal report describing a particular act, was that prosecutor bound by the legal assessment made by the police?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Of course not. The police, as a rule, would provide a legal qualification of the act without consulting the prosecutor. And according to the law, such a legal qualification, and even the description of the act contained in that document, were not binding for the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, could you tell us whether all the documents and information about an event were the only basis for the action of the competent prosecutor, or did he have to consult the police before proceeding?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, the prosecutor, in line with the law, has the right to request additional information to be collected by the police, and all this with a view to check out in greater detail whether there is any grounds to suspect that a criminal act had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The decision of the prosecutor, should he find that there was no act committed or if he asked for additional information or to continue with the investigations, were these decisions his exclusive right or could anyone else make that decision on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No. That was something that only he could decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When, at the request of the prosecutor, criminal proceedings are instituted, tell me, was the court bound by the legal assessment given by the prosecutor, and who establishes definitely how certain acts will be qualified for which a person is charged?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: There is specific provision in the Law on Criminal Procedure which stipulated that the court was not bound in any sense by the qualifications contained in the indictment. He was only bound by the acts and also by the personal information about the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about the situation that you confronted as chief of the security services centre and also as a judge in Zenica in 1993. Tell me, please, this large fluctuation of refugees and others passing through Zenica, was this a cause of problems and difficulties when it came to finding suspects of offences? Was it difficult to identify people? Did you encounter people providing false identification and so on? Did you have this kind of problem, and to what extent was it -- did it make your work more difficult?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such problems, and they did aggravate the conditions for the work of the police. As I have already said, certain parts of the region which formally and legally were the area of responsibility of the security services centre were areas that we physically could not go to. Also, until the 3rd Corps was established, in particular, people in town would move around town in uniform and carrying arms. And it was very difficult to establish the identity of people because they didn't have ID documents. And in view of these circumstances, it was very difficult to file reports of offences as well as crimes under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, you just mentioned certain other reports of offences. Could you explain to Their Honours what forms of responsibility existed within the legal system of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Within the legal system of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war - and this applied during the war as well - there were three forms of accountability for certain illegal acts. The first was a disciplinary offence. The second was an infraction, and the third was criminal liability.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, which of these liabilities was established by the courts or, rather, which court was responsible for which of those offences? And more particularly, which were established before courts as independent judicial bodies?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Disciplinary liability was established by disciplinary bodies within organisations of associated labour or within state institutions or administrative bodies. These would be violations of duties at work. Then infractions were established before magistrates' courts, which were not really courts in the proper sense of the word but more like administrative bodies which would establish people's responsibilities at that level. And finally, criminal liability was established before regular independent courts, and this was regulated by the laws on regular courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, you said that offences were established by magistrates' courts. Tell me ask you first: In which areas would such offences occur, or, rather, which was the main responsibility of these magistrates' courts?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The most frequent offences were disturbances of public law and order, then traffic safety. And within the overall number of such reports, these were the dominant ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where were these magistrate courts for misdemeanors active? In which areas were they established?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: They were established to cover a municipality, which meant that every municipality had a magistrate's court. And then upon appeal there was a council for misdemeanors which existed before the war at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, are you aware whether these magistrate courts were operating in Zenica in 1992 and 1993, and did they process or, rather, try people for violations of public law and order and for other misdemeanors as stipulated by the law?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Zenica municipality, the magistrate court was operating throughout. It never stopped working. There were no interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that criminal acts and criminal liability were debated and established before regular courts as independent judicial bodies. Tell me, which courts existed in Zenica or, rather, what were the competencies of those courts that existed in Zenica while you were a judge?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of regular courts before the war, there was a basic court in Zenica and a higher court. The basic court in the areas of crimes had to try criminal offences for which punishment of up to ten years was envisaged. The higher court dealt with proceedings and charges for which the sanction was more than ten years or even the death penalty. At the beginning of the war, district military courts were also formed, and in Zenica there was one such court, a district military court and also the district military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were a judge of the higher court in Zenica, which means a court which was part of the system of regular courts or, rather, it continued acting in the way it did before the war. Did your courts try individuals including members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a rule, the court tried civilians. But should there be co-perpetrators, if there were co-perpetrators, that is a civilian and a military person, then we would also try the military persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, finally, Mr. Begic, on the basis your own personal experience as a judge and chief of the security services centre, are you aware that members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in 1993, were charged in magistrate courts, district courts, and higher courts? Are you aware of members of the army being tried in all these courts for various acts which allegedly they had committed?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that they were taken to magistrate courts and regular courts, and I personally tried certain members of the army and found them guilty, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that brings to an end my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is half past three. We will now have the so-called technical break, and we will resume at five to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do the Defence counsel of the other team, do they have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just now we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would the Prosecution be kind enough to begin with their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here today we represent the Prosecution in this case, and I have some questions that we'd like to ask you. And as the Presiding Judge told you earlier, if any of my questions are incomprehensible or you don't understand them, just tell me that and I will be more than happy to rephrase the question. My purpose here, as you're probably aware, is not in any way to confuse you but simply to put some additional questions to you. Let me turn first to the investigation, if you will, into the events in Dusina. My learned colleague showed you four documents including some that related to paraffin testing. I believe you actually still have those documents in front of you. Let me ask you this, sir: How was it that CSB Zenica became involved in the events in Dusina or looking at the events in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, this happened at the request of the investigating judge of the district military court in Zenica. This was also the result of the fact that military security bodies were not properly equipped nor did they have the necessary manpower to perform certain acts, certain tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time, sir, when the investigating judge from the district military court in Zenica -- I guess, did he approach you or phone you? How did -- how was he first in contact with you?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Not with me in person as the chief of the centre, but I know that the normal way to communicate was through the duty Operations Officer of the security services centre. Now, if the duty officer was directly called up by the judge of the military court or whether the call came from a member of the military police is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you first recall approximately when you became aware of these events in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I learnt about them on the date of the funeral of these people. As far as I can remember, this happened in the area of Zenica, that is a locality called Cajdras. And this was a very specific event in the security sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, other than the documents that you've looked at which indicate paraffin tests being done, what other type of assistance did CSB Zenica provide to the investigating judge of the district military court of Zenica with respect to the events that occurred in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Apart from this, I am not aware of any other kind of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you're not aware of or you don't recall any witness statements being taken or any steps being taken to identify or interview eyewitnesses to these events?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. If this did happen, then it should have been at the request of the investigating judge of the military court or at the request of the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir, based on your experience as a judge in Zenica: Can you describe for us a little bit about any procedures that your aware of with respect to amnesties or pardons for individuals convicted of crimes who had served in the ABiH from 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I am aware that a law on amnesty was passed. I'm not able to tell you when exactly this law was passed. And it generally amnestied all perpetrators of crimes that were members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that there were exceptions. The pardon could not apply to all criminal acts, I don't think. Certainly not in the case of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you perhaps enlighten us as to the legal effect of this type of pardon in the sense of, did it eliminate the conviction? What was the status of the pardon? What did it mean in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: If the criminal proceedings were undergoing and no effective sentence had been passed, the proceedings would be stopped. If it was in the sentencing stage, then a sentence would be passed whereby the charges are rejected. If there was a sentence and a prison term was ruled, then that would be withheld. The prison term would be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact that my learned friend is asking certain questions from an area that I did not discuss with the witness during the examination-in-chief, in accordance with the Rules of the cross-examination, the Prosecutor should lay the grounds for embarking upon these questions and to indicate to what extent that would be in contradiction with what the witness has said. I am referring to the Rule 90(ii). The Rule is Rule 90(ii), paragraph (ii). 2

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With all due respect to my colleague, the last set of questions or question she put to the witness concerned whether or not any soldiers had in fact been tried before the civilian courts, and his testimony was there were cases where soldiers were tried and there were cases where civilian and soldier co-perpetrators were tried, and of course that is clearly, if you will, clearly opens the door for us to ask him questions about this. I should also alert the Trial Chamber or seek leave from the Trial Chamber that we are planning on cross-examining this witness on a number of issues relating to the use of the courts that he was familiar with for the prosecution of such persons and such individuals, and it's our view that although this specific question might not fall within the Rule 90(ii), certainly the Defence asked him questions about whether soldiers were in fact prosecuted before the courts, of which this witness sat as a judge, and so and we believe that this line of questioning we're about to embark on clearly fits within the proper scope of Prosecution examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It appears that the Defence asked the witness questions as a jurist whether soldiers were prosecuted and judged, and the witness said "yes." So the Prosecution is quite right to ask whether all persons were put on trial, and if not, why. And they referred to the law on amnesty. So, Mr. Mundis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you did tell us that there were cases where soldiers were, in fact -- or ABiH members were in fact tried before the high court in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, of instances where soldiers had been tried by that court but those judgements were subsequently quashed because the case should have been before the district military court?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that those would have been cases where there weren't civilian co-perpetrators involved? It was solely ABiH member or members who were involved in the crimes?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The status of a military person could have been debatable, and then the court that would rule on appeal, in our case the Supreme Court, would rule that the status of the person had not been proven or, rather, that he is a military man and that he should be tried by the district military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the instance that you've just been telling us about where we're -- where an issue is -- concerns the status of the person who is accused or in cases where soldiers were granted some kind of pardon or amnesty, how was the status of the individual established before the courts in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: On the basis of evidence regarding that fact. And the evidence could be and was, as a rule, a certificate from the administrative body, the Secretariat of Defence, indicating that the man was a military person. So all members of the army needed to be registered with those bodies, and those bodies would issue such certificates. And they would inform the court, at its request, about that if there was any dispute about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a person named Zajko Kozlic?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us who Mr. Kozlic is?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Zajko Kozlic is also a law graduate who, before the war was employed as a military man, as an officer in the Yugoslav People's Army, and he had a degree in law. Sometime during the war, I don't know exactly when, he was elected to the position of judge of the basic court in Zenica, and he remained in that position until this year, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of Adil Smailagic?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He's my colleague. He was a judge of the cantonal court in Zenica. He's now retired, or, rather, he's now an attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of Safit Adrovic?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was also a judge in the cantonal court. He's now retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at any time in the period 1992 through 1995, were you aware of any cases involving an individual by the name of Ramo Durmis?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that the case was tried at the higher court in Zenica. It was against him and some other persons as co-perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you recall any of the specific instances or the specific facts of that case that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I just know that the case was tried in court. I was not involved in any sense as a judge in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have some documents which fall into the category of new documents which I would like to show to this witness. We are in a position to answer the questions which the Trial Chamber previously has directed us to answer with respect to any new documents. In the event that this will lead to argumentation, we would respectfully request that the witness be temporarily removed from the courtroom. These documents were provided to the Defence prior to the commencement of today's session and were disclosed previously, so the Defence was aware that these documents would be shown to the witness. I don't know what the position of the Defence is, but, again, if this will require argumentation, I would respectfully ask that the witness be taken out the courtroom, but perhaps the Defence can tell us what their position is, and I'm, of course, in a position to answer the questions that the Trial Chamber has with respect to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will ask the witness to be escorted out the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps while that's being done, Mr. President, for the sake of Your Honours and of course for the Defence, at the time the Chamber rendered its provisional decision with respect to the use of new documents, we were directed to answer a few questions and allow me to do that now. What we have, Mr. President, are four documents which come from the high court in Zenica or the district military court in Zenica. The source of these documents was, actually, what is now known as the Cantonal Court in Zenica. The Office of the Prosecution submitted a request for assistance to the Bosnian authorities on 9 September, 2004, which was after the close of the Prosecution case requesting all court files and materials relating to Mr. Ramo Durmis. We received two batches of such material from the Bosnian authorities. The first batch on 13 October 2004, and the second batch on 11 November 2004. The four documents in question were part of the material that was received in the first batch, that is the Prosecution received it on 13 October 2004. That material was then processed internally. The original Bosnian-language documents from the first batch were disclosed on the 15th of November, 2004. The English translations of the four documents that we are proposing to show to the witness was received from the translation section on the 26th of November, 2004, and immediately disclosed to the Defence on the 26th of November, 2004. As I previously informed the Chamber a few moments ago, we informed the Defence of our intention to show these documents to the witness depending upon the answers to the questions put to him in cross-examination prior to today's -- immediately prior to today's session, and we did provide, again, copies of the four documents that we are proposing to show to two Defence teams shortly before today's session commenced, but we're talking here the four documents in total are approximately 12 to 15 pages of material that is contained within this. I should also alert the Chamber to the fact that of the material in the two batches that we did receive, there is additional material which is being -- currently being translated, and of course the English translations will be disclosed to the Defence as soon as possible. These four documents relate to -- one is a request for the commencement of an investigation, two of them are judgements, and one of them is a ruling terminating detention, and they all relate to Mr. Ramo Durmis. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To summarise, there are four documents that have to do with Mr. Ramo Durmis. One document is a decision on terminating detention. There is one judgement, and there are two requests. The Prosecution says that they requested they be provided with these documents in September 2004, and the Prosecution disclosed or has disclosed some of the documents to the Defence. This was done on the 15th of November, 2004. And today, the Prosecution informed Defence counsel of their intention to show this witness the documents referred to. The Chamber rendered a provisional decision. Tomorrow we will be rendering our oral decision. Mr. Bourgon, I'll give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will give the floor to my colleague, and if necessary, I may add some comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, the position of both Defence teams is that these documents should not be permitted to be shown to the witness at this stage. As Your Honour has indicated, Your Honour's decision on this matter is being rendered tomorrow, and we would suggest that the proper course would be to consider the documents in light of your decision and for us then to be able to, in light of that decision, present what our objections might be to these very late documents, and I underline that, very late documents being shown to the witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I said that we should be rendering our decision tomorrow, but we could do so immediately. Mr. Bourgon -- yes, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I do think that the proper course would be for that decision to be rendered first, and I would ask that Your Honours then hear the Defence in relation to these particular documents once Your Honours have rendered that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, is there anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Not at this point in time, if the Trial Chamber is about to render its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will withdraw now. --- Break taken at 4.23 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Given the issue raised by the fact that the Prosecution presented four new documents, given this fact, the Trial Chamber will now render its oral decision. We were going to render a decision tomorrow, but we have to deal with the issue immediately. I have provided the oral decision to the interpreters who will interpret it. We could also provide a written copy to those who want a copy after it has been read out. I'll read the decision out slowly so that everyone can follow. On the 9th of November, 2004, Defence counsel made an oral motion and requested that the Trial Chamber forbid the Prosecution to use new documents in the course of its cross-examination after the presentation of its case. See pages 11467 to 11474 of the transcript. Having heard this motion, the Trial Chamber, on the 10th of November, 2004, granted the Prosecution 15 days to respond. See page 11484 of the transcript. On the 10th of November, 2004, the Trial Chamber also requested that the Prosecution inform it of the source of the documents, the date on which the documents were obtained, and the circumstances under which the Prosecution obtained these documents after the presentation of its case. See page 11517 of the transcript. On the 24th of November, 2004, the Prosecution responded orally to the motion made by the Defence on the 9th of November, 2004, and the Prosecution provided the information requested by the Trial Chamber on the 10th of November, 2004. See pages 12208 to 12218. The Defence responded orally to the Prosecution's response on the very same day. See pages 12218 to 12232. The reason for this debate between the parties is that the Prosecution produced documents that they hadn't requested to be tendered into evidence when presenting their case, and they did this in the course of examining witnesses for the Defence. Thus the Prosecution presented new documents at hearings on the 26th of October, the 28th of October, the 5th of November, and the 9th of November, 2004. See pages 10616 to 10629, 10918 to 10923, 11235 to 11238, and 11466 to 11467 of the transcript. First of all, the Trial Chamber would like to summarise the main issues raised by the parties. The Prosecution claims that they provided to the Defence the relevant documents that supported the allegations made in the indictment. The Prosecution also says, or claims, that when the Defence was presenting its evidence, the Defence raised certain issues that hadn't been covered by the Prosecution. For example, there were crimes committed by the HVO referred to. As a result, the Prosecution may present documents that relate to questions put to witnesses by the Defence that the Prosecution had not planned to present. The Prosecution also adds that in the course of the trial, it is continuing with investigations and thus it can add new documents that might be admitted after the presentation of its case. The Prosecution also referred to a decision rendered in the Kupreskic case, IT-95-16-T on the 25th of June, 1999. The Defence responded that the Prosecution had the burden of proof and that it should not produce new documents in order to protect itself in the light of arguments presented by the Defence. Defence counsel admits that the Rules do not specifically refer to the rules that would govern cross-examination, and the Defence believes that the rights of the accused mean that one should not interpret these rules in a manner that would be advantageous to the Prosecution. And the Prosecution, pursuant to Rule 65 ter (iii), must disclose to the Defence all the documents that it has. The Defence believes that if the Prosecution has certain documents in its possession, it may only present these documents in the course of its rebuttal. It is at this stage that the Prosecution has the right to present new evidence. The Defence adds that there are exceptions to this rule. Firstly, one is exempt from this Rule if the Prosecution believes that the credibility of the witness could be brought into question. And secondly -- the second exception concerns cases where the Prosecution wants to present a document in order to refresh the witness's memory. The way in which evidence is presented pursuant to the Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Chamber would also like to point out that admitting a document into evidence does not amount to attaching certain weight to this document. It does not amount to attaching a definitive weight to the document at the end of the trial. The Trial Chamber would like to indicate that there is a principle which is fundamental and which must be respected by the Prosecution, and that is that the Prosecution must present all its evidence in the course of its case. This is a rule that is present in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. See, for example, paragraph 14 of the decision rendered on the 31st of October, 2000 by the Trial Chamber in the Kunarac case, and paragraph 5 of the decision dated the 10th of September, 2004, rendered by the Trial Chamber in the Strugar case. As a result of this principle, the Prosecution can only present in the course of its cross-examination of a witness new documents that have not been admitted -- it may present new documents only if it wants to reinforce evidence that it has presented already or if it wants to introduce new elements that concern the criminal responsibility of the accused. In particular, the Trial Chamber rejects the arguments of the Prosecution, according to which the Prosecution should be granted more freedom to produce documents that have not already been admitted into evidence because the Prosecution claims that they could not wait for the Defence to present its evidence that concerns the interpretation of the historical context, the political and the military context, for example, the crimes committed by the HVO. The Trial Chamber would like to draw the Prosecution's attention to paragraphs 10 and 11 of the pre-trial brief for Mr. Amir Kubura, dated the 3rd of November, 2003, and also to paragraph 17 and 24 of the pre-trial brief of Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic, dated the 3rd of November, 2003. Reference in these pre-trial briefs is made to the military and political context of this specific case. In addition, the Trial Chamber would like to point out that the documents mentioned above produced by the Prosecution on the 26th of October, the 28th of October, and the 5th of November, and the 9th of November, 2004, do not relate to the general context of the case. Nevertheless, there are two matters in which the Prosecution may request that new evidence be admitted after the presentation of its case. Firstly, the Prosecution may make such request in the rebuttal stage, and pursuant to Rule 85(A)(iii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and also in accordance with the manner for tendering such documents into evidence described in paragraph 273 of the Celebici judgement dated the 20th of February, 2001. Secondly, it may request that its case be reopened under the conditions provided for in paragraph 283 of the Celebici judgement, and paragraph 12 of the decision of the 4th of May, 2001, rendered by the Trial Chamber in the Krstic case. The Trial Chamber would like to point out that the scope of cross-examination is limited by Rule 90(H)(i) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. According to this Rule, cross-examination should be limited to the following points unless otherwise decided by the Chamber. It must be limited to issues raised in the course of the examination-in-chief, or it must be limited to issues that have to do with the credibility of the witness, or it must be limited to points that are part of the case of the party that is conducting the cross-examination. In addition, Article 90(H)(ii) says that in the cross-examination a witness who is able to give evidence for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case for the party for whom that counsel appears. The scope of cross-examination of a witness by the Prosecution is thus limited to the points referred to in Rule 90(H) of the Rules. In the course of such cross-examination, the Prosecution may naturally confront the witness or may present to the witness any documents that have already been admitted into evidence. The Prosecution may present and request that certain documents be tendered into evidence, if these documents have not already been admitted into evidence, in the course of cross-examination, but the conditions will be much more restricted and will be governed by the principles that have already been referred to. In the opinion of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution may present, in the course of its cross-examination, any documents that have not already been admitted in order to test the credibility of a witness or to refresh such a witness's memory. In each of these two cases, the Prosecution may present a document that has not already been admitted and which it had in its possession before or after the presentation of its case. The Trial Chamber is of the opinion that when the Prosecution plans to present such a document in the course of its preparatory work, that it must disclose such a document to the Defence, and it must inform the Defence of its intention to present such a document at least 24 hours before a Defence witness appears, unless the Defence has provided the Prosecution with the information they need to prepare their cross-examination a little too late. The Prosecution may request the admission into evidence of a document that it has disclosed provided that it is in order to establish the credibility of a witness or to refresh a witness's memory. And such a document can only be admitted in a limited manner and can only be used to establish the credibility of the oral testimony of the witness or to refresh the witness's memory. The Trial Chamber would like to draw the parties' attention to documents P103 and P106, which admitted in this limited manner following a decision rendered on the 16th of July, 2004. With regard to this matter, the Trial Chamber would like to point out that document P931 was tendered into evidence on the 27th of October, 2004, at the request of the Prosecution when cross-examining the Defence witness Siljak Remzija. This is what is stated on page 10618 of the transcript. The Prosecution present this had document to establish the credibility of the witness Siljak. As a result, the Trial Chamber confirms the admission of this document but would like to point out that this document is being admitted only in order to determine the credibility of the oral testimony of Witness Siljak. The Trial Chamber would also like to point out that document P935 -- P935 was presented on the 5th of November, 2004, at the request of the Prosecution when cross-examining the Defence witness Haris Jusic. As we can see on pages 11235 and 11238 of the transcript, the Prosecution presented this document in order to refresh the witness's memory. As a result, the Trial Chamber would like to confirm that this document is being admitted into evidence, but we would like to point out that it is being admitted in order to refresh the memory of the witness Jusic. So that's our four-page decision, and having read the decision out, in the light of this decision is there anything the Prosecution would like to say? Would the Prosecution like to show its documents to the witness? Mr. Mundis, if you have understood the decision, if not, you may take the time to examine it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we have understood the decision, although certainly some additional time to read and reflect on the full extent of the Chamber's order might be helpful. In light of, however, what the witness has said with respect to -- what he's testified here concerning Mr. Ramo Durmis and the case involving him, it would certainly be our position that the documents which we were proposing to show to him would certainly be of assistance in refreshing his recollection with respect to these events in question. And our preliminary view, again without having time to reflect and re-read the transcript with respect to the Trial Chamber's decision, our position would be that the four documents we were planning on showing to this witness would certainly fall within the scope of refreshing recollection with respect to his testimony and the fact that he said he was aware that Mr. Durmis had been prosecuted but didn't recall the specifics. So that would be our preliminary position with respect to showing this witness these four documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Contrary to what my learned friend from the Prosecution says, we oppose this position in conformity with the decision of the Chamber. The decision of the Chamber does not allow the Prosecution to show a document to the witness to refresh his memory, but the witness has already answered questions and said what he knows about the event.
