He said he was not implicated in it, so there's no other subject remaining in doubt regarding the memory of this witness regarding this event. For these reasons, Mr. President, I think that these four documents cannot be shown to this witness. The question posed by the Prosecution within the framework of these documents, in my view, the subject is closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I agree with my learned friend Mr. Bourgon that these documents come nowhere near falling into the category of memory refreshing and it would be pushing Your Honours' judgement to the limit to try to introduce them on that basis. I refer Your Honours to page 34, line 25, of the transcript where the witness said quite clearly that all he knows is that there was this case tried in court, and he says, "I was not involved in any sense as a judge in that case." So in our submission, there would be no point showing these documents to the witness to refresh his memory as he have not involved in the case. There is nothing to refresh, Your Honours. If one of the persons who he mentioned, namely the investigating judge or the prosecutor were here as a witness, well, that might be a different matter altogether, that those persons might remember the matter. They might need to have their memories refreshed. But this particular judge was not involved and is not somebody who could comment on these documents in any way whatsoever. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is going to withdraw to deliberate. The question is quite simple, and it is as follows: The Prosecution, pursuant to our ruling, believes that it can produce these four documents to refresh the witness's memory. The Defence tells us there's no reason to refresh the witness's memory as the case referred to by the documents was not a case that was addressed by this witness, and consequently, there's no -- nothing to refresh his memory about, because the witness on page 34, line 24, said that he was not aware of this case. So we will withdraw. It will not take long. We will be back in a few minutes. --- Break taken at 5.04 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is rendering another oral decision in answer to the question whether the Prosecution is allowed to produce four new documents and to show them to the witness to refresh his memory. In view of the observations made by the Defence, it is the opinion of the Chamber that in view of the fact that this witness was not familiar with the case of Mr. Ramo Durmis, he cannot -- his memory cannot be refreshed. Otherwise, this would have been possible if he was involved. So there's no possibility of refreshing his memory and, therefore, the Prosecution cannot show him these documents. We're going to bring the witness back in to continue with the cross-examination. If we don't finish today, we can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the hearing continues. We had to have an interruption, and we had to ask you to leave the courtroom because we had to address a procedural matter, and we rendered two oral decisions, and now I will give the floor again to the Prosecution to continue their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in response to some questions put to you by the Defence, you told us about foreigners who were in the area of Zenica in 1992 and 1993, and you told us about the difficulties because these persons weren't registered with CSB. Do you recall talking about that?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection in the period of 1992 up until the time in February 1993 when you left CSB Zenica to become a high court judge, do you recall any instances in which CSB Zenica was involved in investigating any crimes committed by such foreigners?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Just now I do not recollect any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's go back, then, sir, to the subject or -- or let's turn now to the subject of the cooperation between CSB Zenica and the 3rd Corps. You told us that due to the lack of proper equipment and some of the lack of training of military police within the 3rd Corps, CSB actively cooperated with units of the 3rd Corps. Is that a fair summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Cooperation with a view to carrying out our duties. If you mean that, then that is my answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's what I mean, sir. The cooperation, as you put it, with a view to carrying out your duties. Can you tell us a little bit about how this cooperation worked in practice, what types of crimes or what types of investigative work you would be doing in cooperation with the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: It was mostly or exclusively engaging our department for crime technology. If an act came under the competence of the military court, the operative procedures were carried out by the military security body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say this cooperation was mostly or exclusively engaging your department for crime technology, I take it then from that that you weren't providing the type of assistance such as interviewing witnesses or interviewing victims or anything like that? It was more related to technical assistance?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, any of the specific units of the 3rd Corps that you provided this type of technical assistance to?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I've already said that we cooperated with the military police battalion, which was operating within the framework of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the 3rd Corps military police battalion, did you have any involvement with 3rd Corps security department or with any other units of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the types -- or first of all, approximately on how many instances of the formation of the 3rd Corps until you departed CSB Zenica in February 1993, on how many occasions do you recall providing the 3rd Corps military police battalion with technical assistance?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I would sign certain documents coming from the CSB and going towards other bodies, because I represented that centre of security service. As for the contents of those documents, I didn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, sir, I take it, then, from your last answer that you can't help us with respect to any specific crimes or alleged crimes that CSB Zenica provided assistance to 3rd Corps other than Dusina, which we've spoken about?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: In concrete terms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about any problems that CSB Zenica might have encountered in its relations or cooperation with the 3rd Corps? Do you recall any instances where there was difficulties or where the cooperation wasn't operating smoothly?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't recollect any particular case or any particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving any documents from the Ministry of the Interior concerning cooperation or attempts to improve cooperation between CSB Zenica and the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I think there were documents that spoke in general terms about the relationship between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Ministry of the Interior, but something specific about the Zenica CSB and the 3rd Corps, I don't recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, earlier in response to a question from my learned colleague from the Defence, you told us a little bit about how the reserve police could be resubordinated to the army during wartime on certain occasions. Can you describe for us the -- whether it was possible for the Ministry of the Interior as a whole to be subordinated to the military during wartime?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: According to the law on defence or, rather, on service of the armed forces, the Presidency was the Supreme Commander. Now, whether the Presidency could have passed such a decision is something I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you're not aware of any specific order of the Presidency doing such a thing during the war in 1993?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any specific instances where you had -- you experienced any difficulties concerning issues that might be considered jurisdictional issues between CSB Zenica and the 3rd Corps or any of its subordinates units?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, I cannot recollect any particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us earlier, again in response to a question from my learned colleague from the Defence, that there were certain areas within the region that CSB Zenica covered to which you did not have access. Can you be more specific in terms of what area or areas that fell within the jurisdiction of CSB Zenica that you did not have access to?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I have already listed some areas, and I will repeat. That was the case with respect to Busovaca, in the first place, also Vitez, Zepca. I think also Donji Vakuf, Gornji -- no, Donji, Donji Vakuf, from the beginning, yes. From the very beginning of the war. And some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution would respectfully ask to be permitted to address a couple of questions to the witness that fall outside the scope of the direct examination concerning the Islamic centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Chamber renders its decision, the Prosecution wishes to ask the witness questions about the Islamic centre of Zenica. This centre has cropped up on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, we would like to know why the Prosecutor wishes to put these questions to the witness, because he said himself that this was not covered by the examination-in-chief. And secondly, according to the personal data of this witness, I see no link between then witness and such questions. So we have to know why he wishes to put these questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we fully support what Mrs. Residovic has said, and we have nothing more to add. We don't understand why our learned friend wishes to ask those questions at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber can always allow all questions if they feel that these questions are of interest. So tell us, what is the interest of this question, noting that the Defence has said that nothing in the CV or the answers or the status of this witness allows us to suppose that he can produce any useful answers about this Islamic centre. Perhaps the Prosecutor, however, can enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, during the course of the searches that we do on the witnesses, there is a document that we have from a later period in time which contains a reference to a person with the same name as this witness, and I don't know if it is in fact the same person or perhaps someone with the same name. And again, the document is dated from, I believe, 1996, and we would simply like to ask the witness a couple of questions to determine if, in fact, there is any link whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to retreat again for a few minutes. --- Break taken at 5.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is going to render another oral decision regarding allowing the Prosecution to put a question to the witness that was not within the scope of the examination-in-chief. The Prosecution tells us that they have a document in their possession bearing the first and last name of the witness, a document about this Islamic centre. The Chamber notes that this Islamic centre has already been referred to during several testimonies, and in view of that, it is in the interest of justice to check the correspondence between the Islamic centre and the witness. So, Mr. Mundis, you have the floor to ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the period from 1992 through 1993, were you affiliated in any way with the Islamic centre in Zenica in terms of being an official, on the board of directors, or in any way affiliated with the Islamic centre?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions for the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Re-examination, please. I'm looking at the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Begic, relating to the questions put you by my learned friend in connection with the question of amnesty or pardon, tell me, please, is an amnesty an act of the court or is it something regulated by law?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Amnesty is granted exclusively on the basis of a law adopted by the Assembly. Or in wartime, this was done by the Presidency with the force of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, is an amnesty an act of mercy or does it annul court decisions that had previously established responsibility of a certain accused who was properly tried and sentenced?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Without entering into the reasons for an amnesty, generally speaking it can be described as an act of mercy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about cooperation with the military police battalion and the CSB, you can speak about that cooperation for the time period when you were in the CSB, or do you know anything about it also as a judge of the high court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I can speak about it while I performed both those duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Referring to the period when you were in the CSB, tell us, what kinds of crimes did you come across as the security services centre as well as the military police, and were those acts that required the kind of cooperation that you have described?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Of course. That cooperation through the involvement of the criminal technology department mainly -- was mainly developed in the case of manslaughter, when certain technologies were required. Also in forensic studies of fingerprints in the case of thefts and burglaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you can remember that time period, can you tell us what was the name of those crimes? What types of crimes did you cooperate on with the military police?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: In the case of manslaughter, murder, then in the case of serious burglaries, theft. In the case of the crime of rape our assistance again was indispensable for forensic examination of traces that are required in such instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you could recall such cooperation while you were a judge of the high court. Tell me, were you ever in a situation when a military police battalion -- when the military battalion of the 3rd Corps rejected a request that you or any colleague of yours may have made with respect to the military police?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any such instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, can you recall the number of members of the army that appeared before the relevant courts in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I am not -- I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you about various types of crimes. You have just now mentioned murder, rape, burglaries, thefts, et cetera. Earlier on, you said that the legal qualification depended on the court. Tell me, as a judge confronting such crimes, did you give thought to whether those crimes contained any elements of a war crime against the civilian population? And if you did not, tell me, on what grounds would you decide that an act was one of the crimes you have listed?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that in my experience, there were no cases when I had any such dilemmas. These were mostly individual instances of violence, so that I never had any thoughts that this might be a war crime. My answer is a very general one without referring to any particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a moment, please. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the last question, in our respectful view, is beyond the scope of the cross-examination, but the witness has since answered the question, so I'll withdraw any objection that we may have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you just one more question. In answer to a question from my learned friend, you said that a judge could have some hesitation as to the status of a suspect. Tell me, in such a situation, would the judge produce evidence in support of this?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I think I have already answered that question when I said that the court would seek additional information from the defence secretariat who had information about members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If it's the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, let me ask you this: As chief of the CSB and later as a judge, you did cooperate with the military police battalion. Do you know whether that battalion investigated and filed criminal reports for all these various crimes, also with regard to other units of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I do know that it did, because I acted in certain cases when the military police battalion submitted a report. These were cases on appeal with respect to rulings of the district military court, and this belonged to the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're now going to have the break, and when we resume at 6.00 p.m., I will ask the other Defence team whether they have any additional questions, after which the Judges will have their questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the other Defence team have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have only two questions in order to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, when you mentioned the crimes covered by the amnesty, you said that not all crimes were covered by this amnesty, and you said that crimes of war were not covered by the amnesty.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And murder, rape, and aggravated theft were also not covered by the amnesty?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And my second question is: When you mentioned crimes in which there was an amnesty, you said that in cases when there was a sentence, you said in such a case the accused was not to serve the sentence. The sentence remained, though. It wasn't amended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have a few questions and then the other Judges will also ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that you were the chief of the police, of the civilian police, in Zenica. Can you confirm that up until February, at least, you were in charge of the civilian police that was under the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: How many policemen did you have? You were in charge of how many policemen in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Only in Zenica or in all the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Zenica and in the entire region.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but perhaps there were up to 5.000 men. These were staff members who were authorised and who didn't have authority [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had 5.000 men. And what about the men who were capable of carrying out judicial investigations? Out of the 5.000 men, how many such men were there?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify something. Not all the policemen could carry out judicial investigations. Only those who were assigned to certain departments for crime detection could get involved in such investigations. Most of the policemen were in uniform and, in fact, their task was to maintain public law and order. They didn't have the authority to carry out investigations into crimes that had been perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir. The department are responsibility for identifying crimes and misdemeanors, how many men were there in that department?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact number, but perhaps there were up to about ten of them. Up to about ten men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were ten of them who covered the entire region. Let's take a simple example. A crime is committed. Someone is found dead in their house. Someone was killed in their house. Who carries out the investigation? Are you informed of the crime as the chief? And who will go to carry out the initial on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, the operations officer in the CSB is informed of the crime. He then forms a team to carry out an on-site investigation if this is necessary. And the operations officer informs the investigating judge and the prosecutor. It is the investigating judge who is in charge of the investigation. The investigating judge is in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's imagine that a number of individuals who have been killed are found. The duty officer -- does the duty officer submit a report to you as the chief of the civilian police? Aren't you informed of the fact that at a certain site a certain number of bodies were found? Were you not personally informed of such cases?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I was informed of such cases by means of bulletins that I as the chief of the centre received on a daily basis, but I wasn't immediately informed of the crimes committed. I wasn't informed of the fact in order to decide how a team to carry out an on-site investigation would be formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But when the investigating judge carries out the investigation, he is not able to do everything himself. He has to ask the police to help him to identify the individuals, carry out paraffin tests, autopsies, et cetera. When the phase of the department for carry investigation of crimes is completed and the documents are forwarded to judges, do you sign documents, do you submit anything to the judges stating that in the course of the investigation such-and-such things were done?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, there's the chief of the CSB. I signed all of the documents that were forwarded to other individuals, other bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now show you a document -- a document shown to you by the Defence. We will have a look at P332. It's dated the 1st of February, and it's a document that you signed.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was sent to the district military court. Why doesn't it contain the name of the prosecutor or the judge? Why does the document only refer to the district military court? Why are the judge and prosecutor not mentioned? Why did you just note down "District military court" in the heading?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a letter from the CSB to the military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But when signing this document, you didn't know who would read the document, who would receive it.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, the president of the court decides about this. He knows which judges will be assigned to a particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were a judge; you are a lawyer. When one has a look at this document, does this document contain reference to an investigation of any kind? Because this document has to do with identification. It's a note on identification. But a body may be identified without there being a crime. Somebody may die of natural causes, and this will not result in an investigation. So how would you describe this document, the letter that you sent to the military court? Did this concern an investigation or is it just an administrative document that was forwarded at your level? When you signed such a document what did you have in mind at the time of signing the document? What did you think about it?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted the document to be forwarded that referred to the work carried out by CSB members, and this was at the request of the authorised investigating judge, the chief of the centre. If was not necessary for me to know which investigating judge had made such a request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said at the request of the authorise the investigating judge. A minute ago you said that a judge had made the request. But how is it that in this document no reference is made to an investigating judge? I can't see the reference to someone's request or someone's instructions. There's no such reference in the document.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I think you can see this in the documents that were attached to this document. This is an additional document. But the annexes listed here are attached to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have a look at as annex P341, which is the paraffin test, dated the 29th of January. The document number is 19102233. When you signed such a document -- or when you sign such a document, do you first read the document on the paraffin test? This paraffin test document was signed by the expert Adzic and by yourself. You signed the document. Did you read the document on the paraffin test? Did you read the entire document? If you didn't read it, you can read it now.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't read the document, nor did I read such documents. I didn't concern myself with the contents of the documents that were presented to me. As a rule, I did not read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you would sign such documents without reading them.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the expert report, the analysis was carried out by an authorised worker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When we read through the paraffin analysis, we won't go into all the details, you're a professional, we the Judges are aware of the fact. We could discuss the matter, but I don't want to go into the technical details. But in this document and with regard to the bodies that were identified, for most of the bodies the test was positive. So particles were found either on the left land -- on their left hand or their right hands. But there is someone calls Pero Ljubicic, and apparently his left hand and his right hand were both negative. As chief of the police, you weren't familiar with this problem? Because if the test was negative, one can conclude that he didn't shoot. If he didn't shoot, why was he dead? Didn't this idea occur to you?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I said I didn't read the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that you didn't read the documents you signed without reading the document.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in your opinion, it's the investigating judge or the prosecutor who should take action on the basis of the document, and as far as you were concerned, it wasn't for you to express your particular opinion.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As chief of the police, did you ever go to the hospital? Did you ever go to the morgue in the hospital to see the corpses there? Did you ever go to see the corpses, you as the chief of the police?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No. I never went there as the chief of police. My duties were such that I couldn't get involved in such operations. There were authorised officials who were responsible for such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In document P333 -- P334 -- have a look at it. It's signed by Enes Saric. The date is the 29th of January. And he describes the body identified. We can see there is Faruk Turkic, a pathologist. There's the HVO, who were also present, represented by Mr. Enver Nesirovic. There's a security officer from the hospital, Mr. Bektas. There are family members. Some names are listed there. When you read such a document, didn't you wonder how it -- why the HVO was interested in this case? Wouldn't you have reacted in this way as chief of the police? Because this document states that the HVO was present in an official capacity. Didn't this show that there might have been a slight problem.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: If I had paid attention to the document, if I had read through it, perhaps that would have occurred it me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you didn't read the document. Similarly, document P333, dated the 29th of January, which concerns the identification of certain individuals. Well, we can see who was in the identification team. There was Dr. Turkic, and there was -- there were the judges and the prosecutor. When the prosecutor goes to the morgue, it means it's an important case, unless the prosecutor of the district military court went to the morgue whenever someone died. How would you explain the fact that he was present at the morgue, especially since your subordinate was present? Because it says that an officer from your centre was present. If the prosecutor is there, how come the chief of the police is not there too? Could you explain this fact?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't explain that, but all I can say is that I was never present in such cases as the chief of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We know that there was a war, and naturally there were a lot of people who had been killed, but was it customary to have in the Zenica hospital's morgue, well, eight bodies listed here. Eight persons were killed. Were there that many people who were killed every day as a result of the conflict or was this an exceptional case? You who were present in the era, what is your opinion of that? Were about ten people killed every day in Zenica or was this an exceptional case?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time as a result of the fighting, there would be far more individuals killed. They would then be transported -- transferred to the hospital before they prepared -- before their funerals were prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to a question awhile ago, you said that you found out that the individuals who were buried at Fafalas [phoen], you said that you found out that an interrogation was carried out into the cause of death. Could you confirm that when you found out about this, you felt that perhaps there was something that should be investigated, that is to say that the circumstances in which these people died should be investigated. Do you remember how this case was presented to you, and did you think, "Well, I signed a document about these individuals." Do you remember when this issue was raised with you again?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know this exact period. I don't know when I found out about the exact burial, and I can't say when these things were signed. I can't say exactly. But I found out about the burial -- I remember that because I was informed by the chief of the public security station that this would be taking place and that certain preparations had been made for security to ensure that the funeral ran smoothly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you found out that there was this burial and that it was necessary to take measures to ensure that there were no problems when these people were buried. But when there is a burial, does the police always take measures? Why in the case of this particular burial was it necessary to take certain measures?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, whenever there is a burial, certain measures must be taken. You have to control the traffic if it's necessary to transport the deceased to the cemetery. But in this case, tension had already risen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that tension had risen. Since you are aware of this fact, didn't you personally have the power to ask the department responsible for identifying crimes and misdemeanors to re-examine the entire case? Wasn't it your responsibility to ask this department to examine all the elements and to try and determine the conditions in which these individuals died? Didn't it occur to you that you should proceed in this manner?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: All I can say is that I didn't think along those lines. If I had, I would have remembered. Now, why I didn't have such thoughts, I can't tell you now. Maybe this was already the period of time when I was leaving the CSB. I would like to mention that as of the 20th of February already I was on annual leave, and I was waiting for a decision to be made regarding the election to the post of judge. I had been proposed by the high court of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You took your position as judge. But the month that followed, and the years that followed, in fact, there wasn't a commission of inquiry? You were never interviewed? No questions were put to you as to the way in which you managed this case?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I also have a few questions on the four documents that have been shown to you. You told us that you were found by an investigating judge from the military court, and that was the beginning of your involvement as a service with this matter. You said also that you could not remember the name of that judge. And you, therefore, directed a letter to the military Tribunal, military court. I have a similar question. In one of these documents, that is P333, 333, there is mention of judges and a prosecutor that has "already been sent by my colleague, who are doing together with a pathologist, Faruk Turkic, in the Zenica CSB forensic office an identification procedure." Please have a look at that document, P333. My question would be -- this would be the first question I would like to put to you: Do you recall or do you not recall who were these judges and who was this prosecutor? Are you still looking for the document?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: This is what I can say: I said that I was not informed directly but that the communication, I assume, went between the investigating judge and the operations duty officer in the CSB who was there to receive requests and forward them on to persons who had to carry out certain activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And then we have --

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: So that I needn't have had the name of the judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I was interrupting you. Sorry. So this has been received via your operations officer. It comes on your desk, or you give the organisation the -- you ask your organisation to cooperate with this judge. Now we see on P333 if you have it -- do you have it now, the document, before you?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, if you see -- if you look at that document, P333, on the second linea, you can see that an identification team is working there. One is a pathologist. That may be someone of your department. There are judges, and there is a prosecutor and a Zenica CSB forensic officer. My question is: Do you remember who these judges were and who the prosecutor was, or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't. It is the person who signed this note who should be able to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right. Continue with the next linea. We read that, "During the identification procedure, a description of the body was taken, the body photographed, and a print of the right index finger taken." In an identification procedure, the whole thing is turning about a question, who is this person that we have found, or who is this person whose body is in here. You take a print of the right index finger. You may do a description of the body. You may also photograph the body. My question to you is: What is the normal standard procedure in such a case? There is a body of an unknown person somewhere in some hospital, and everybody wants to determine who he or she is. You take an index finger. You invite the family if you have an idea who whose family it might be. You take a description of the body. Is photographing a body also part of a standard procedure in your organisation?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. If -- unless a family member recognises the dead person. And in this case, photographs were taken to provide documentary evidence of the external appearance of the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But most of the ten have been recognised by other people. That is evident from the other document, P334. So in that sense there would be no necessity to take a picture, I think, or do the two go together sometimes?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I said that taking a photograph was done to document the external appearance of the body, and this was done by the pathologist, Dr. Faruk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pathologist. I take it he is from the hospital probably. Is he or --

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: He is from the hospital? How would he do that as a pathologist? How would he take photos?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: He makes a report regarding the examination of the body, and our employees were present to prepare the photos, because they had the equipment to be able to do that. So as a rule, the pathologist does not prepare the photo documents. At least that is our practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So your employees take these photographs at the request of this pathologist. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Now, whether it was at the request of the pathologist or the judge -- I assume it would have been at the request of the judge, and to complement the report on the external appearance of the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the whole setting suggests within -- in the presence of a pathologist that these are photographs of people who are naked, so to speak, who have no clothes on the body; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The examination is done when bodies are in that condition, that is, without clothes. The bodies are turned around in various positions, and then photographs are taken so as that this should provide evidence as to the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So that the photographs would show the wounds of the other things that are present on the exterior of the body. The state of the body would be visible from the photographs. That is my question. Is that a correct conclusion?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said already before that you did not read the reports. I take it that you did not look at the photographs in this case either. Is that correct also, or are you seen these pictures of these ten persons?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: As a rule, I didn't look at the photographs. I didn't have time for that as chief of the CSB. I would simply forward the material to the competent official and who was meant to take steps following this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Has there ever been, and maybe you don't know any more because you left the service, but has there been a follow-up request to perform an autopsy? Is this also something you do in your service?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't know with respect to this case. However, as a rule, an autopsy is done if there is suspicion that a crime has been committed. Now, whether an autopsy should be done or not, this is a decision made by the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand that, but you said at the beginning that the investigating judge asks you for an investigation, and since this is an investigation judge, a military investigation judge in this case, I take it that he has reasons to do that and that reason is that he sees the possibility of a crime, and he wants to elucidate the matter further. So --

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge does not undertake such steps only when crimes are committed. The investigating judge will do this also to remove any suspicion of the possibility of a crime, simply to establish the cause of death, and then on that basis to deduce whether it was caused by violence or how it was caused, under which circumstances. These are all things that the investigating judge has to look into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And to what conclusion would that lead in this case? Would you say these are -- have been requests of an investigating judge who thought of the possibility that a crime had been committed or would it be an investigating judge who just wanted to make sure what the cause of the death was?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I am really unable to comment on that, as to what the investigating judge wanted in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I note that he has requested a paraffin test, which is already important, of course. So as far as you remember, there has been no further request for an autopsy. Have you -- have other requests from a military investigating judge at that time or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: While I was chief of the CSB, there were no such requests. Afterwards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question for you, which is linked to what has just been said. In your country at the time, when someone dies, before the burial would it be done as in most -- or several European countries, would there be authorisation for burial but with a medical certificate stating death? Is there someone who comes, according to your laws, to establish death today or before? When someone dies, does the administrative authority issue a death certificate? How does this happen in practice?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are so -- coroners, doctors who examine the person and sign a certificate approving, permitting burial. This is not the case when somebody dies surrounded by family members. Even today, and especially not then did the doctor come to establish death.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in this case, the doctor who needs to issue this certificate, would it not be Dr. Faruk Turkic? He should have issued that, such a certificate?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Faruk Turkic was employed and still is in the cantonal hospital in Zenica, in the pathology department. And if Faruk Turkic examined the bodies, after his examination, he was authorised to issue permission for burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you know, did he do that or not?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Following the Judges' questions, Mr. Mundis, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution does have a few questions in light of those put to the witness by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Prosecution Exhibit P332 which, I believe, is still before you. This is the official note that you signed on the 1st of February, 1993. 1993. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, to the best of your recollection, had there been an autopsy, would you have attached it as one of the annexes to this document that you forwarded to the district military court?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: A report on the autopsy in those days was not drafted by the investigating judge who should do that according to the law on criminal proceedings but, rather, the forensic pathologist would do that. If there was an autopsy, then there should be a record of that autopsy prepared by the forensic pathologist. And if such a report was made, it should have been forwarded to the investigating judge directly by the forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you about the photographs or photo records documenting the appearance of the unidentified persons. You told us that the photos were taken to provide documentary evidence of the external appearance of the body, and my question is: Was that a routine practice or was that done for some particular reason in this specific case?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: In all cases when an external description of the body was done, then there had to be photo documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you told us, with respect to the funeral of these persons, that CSB was involved in terms of providing police and security for the funerals because, as you put it, tensions had risen. I'm wondering if you can elaborate on what you mean by "tensions had risen."

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: One has to bear in mind the period when this was happening, that conflicts between the army and the HVO had already started and that these persons, as far as I know, had lost their lives in such conflicts. The events on the front would be reflected in the town of Zenica itself, and an event of that kind naturally required heightened security measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you be a little more specific, or do you recall -- you just told us, "As far as I know, they had lost their lives in such conflicts." Do you recall any specifics of this incident?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Finally, sir, in response to one of the first questions put to you by the Presiding Judge, you told us that there were 5.000 men within the public security stations in the region covered by CSB Zenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many of those 5.000 persons within CSB Zenica were what one might consider to be armed police officers compared with persons doing other types of work for CSB?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I would say at least about 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: 70 per cent would be armed police officers?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And those police officers would be deployed throughout the municipalities that was covered by CSB Zenica?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Begic, in response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said that among those 5.000 men some of them had authority and others did not. Some were authorised and some were not. Could you tell me what the ratio was among all those employed in the area covered by the CSB? What was the ratio between the authorised men and the unauthorised men?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I think there was 70 per cent of the men who were in uniform, that is to say who had authority, who were authorised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Chamber, you said that you drafted the letter from the CS -- that was sent from the CSB to the district military court. Tell me, were there any rules for those who were to carry out certain professional tasks in the CSB? Was there a department or were there any authorised officials who were responsible for such tasks?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally. As I have already said, we had a department within the CSB, and there was this department for crime technology, or, rather, the forensic department. It was subordinated to the chief of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question about confirming the death of individuals in order to bury these individuals, you said that this was done by coroners, corners would issue certificates, death certificates if a coroner or anyone else believed for any reason that death wasn't caused by natural causes, in such cases was the coroner obliged to inform the police or some other organs?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was his duty to inform the police, and the police would then inform the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you did not inform the judge of a military court or, rather, the investigating judge of the military court and the prosecutor, and awhile ago you said that you thought these individuals who died in combat -- you mentioned these individuals who died in combat, do you remember the prosecutor receiving such information from the military police?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, but I assume that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a number of questions from the Judges, you told us how you carried out certain tasks. To clarify what you said, could you tell us whether the police ever carried out investigations or was it some other body that carried out investigations and, if so, which body?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Officially speaking -- formally speaking, the police never carries out investigations. This is the responsibility of the investigating judge. But the policeman at the request of an investigating judge could carry out certain investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, the investigating judge is the person who orders a certain body to carry out some of the necessary tasks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, and since it wasn't possible for the military police to do this, he requested -- the investigating judge requested that you carry out certain investigations because he could not transfer his duties to other organs, according to the law.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. He could transfer those duties to the military police, but as I have said, at the time the military police did not have the equipment necessary to carry out these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Similarly in response to certain questions, you said that you carried out the actions referred to in the letter or, rather, the documents attached to the letter. Did the investigating judge at the time request that you carry out investigations and take statements from certain individuals?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: While I was the CSB chief, as far as I can remember I never received any such request.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Without having received a request from an investigating judge, could you, in that particular case, carry out such tasks on your own or was it necessary for the investigating judge to make such a request or request a certain organ, you or the military police, to carry out such action?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge had to make such a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the doctor's examination is concerned and as far as the request issued to the pathologist is concerned, which body instructs a doctor to provide a detailed description of a corpse or to perform an autopsy or to assist the judge in any other way? Who is in a position to issue or to make such a request?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Only the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Chamber also asked you about the assessment of the material. Where is all the material -- from whom is all the material collected that various agents collected at the request of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, it's obtained from the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which organ on the basis of all of the material collected assesses whether the event in question is, in fact, a crime, and assesses whether it is necessary to carry out further checks or, rather, whether it's necessary to terminate the case because there's no suspicion of a crime having been perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor decides about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given these legal provisions, on the basis of the documents or, rather, your involvement in that part of the case, would the investigating judge, or did the investigating judge act in accordance with the law and in accordance with the authority he has?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The investigating judge did act in accordance with the law. As to whether he did everything that was necessary to be done -- to be done, this is something that one should assess.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that towards the end of February you went on holiday because the president of the high court in Zenica suggested that you be appointed as a judge. Could you tell me who the president of the Zenica high court was at the time?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Djuro Globlek.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether he was president throughout 1993.

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: Not only through the 1993, but right up until 1995, when he left to work as an assistant in the Ombudsman office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, could you tell me the nationality of the presiding judge?

utterances.speaker: REDZIB BEGIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Defence team have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this concludes your testimony. You've answered all the questions put to you by both the parties and by the Judges. We would like to thank you for your contribution to the truth, and we wish you a good trip home, and we wish you all the best in your new professional career.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few more minutes. I have had a look at the list of documents. Apparently there are two that may be the subject of a request that you may -- that you might be requesting to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, document number 1, 0449, and document number 2, 0544, we would like these documents to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents will be admitted into evidence under the following numbers: DH449, the English version will be DH449/E, and the second document, DH544, the English version will be DH544/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to thank Defence counsel who adhered to the time allocated to them. This enabled us to finish in time. Let's hope that things will proceed similarly tomorrow. Tomorrow we have a witness who will be available for the Chamber, as you know. We'll be sitting in the morning on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. Unfortunately, on Friday the hearing will be in the afternoon. So on Friday, we will be sitting in the afternoon. If there are any changes, you will be informed of them. Thank you, and I will see everyone tomorrow at the hearing at 9.00.
